sections.title: Run the rehearsal
sections.intro: A few days out. Your stories are written. Now turn them into something you can say out loud under pressure.

questions.prompt: What should you rehearse — the exact words, or something else?
options: Only the opening line of each story
The exact script, word for word
Nothing — rehearsing makes you sound robotic
The key points of each beat, not exact wording
questions.explanation: Sounding robotic comes from memorizing wording. Practicing the points you want to hit builds fluency without the stiffness.

questions.prompt: First take: you record yourself telling your leadership story. Reviewing it, what do you check?
options: Only how long the whole thing ran
Only whether the facts are accurate
Pacing, I vs. we, fillers, energy, organization
Lighting, camera angle, and background
questions.explanation: That's the solo review checklist. For example: three minutes in with no actions yet is a pacing failure, and actually counting "we" usually surprises people.

questions.prompt: Playback shows 90 seconds of setup before your first action. What do you fix on take two?
options: Add more Context so it's clearer
Move the setup to after the Results
Cut Context to the stakes — get to an action by ~20s
Speak faster through the same setup
questions.explanation: Aim for about 10% / 60% / 30%. Two or three takes, each fixing what the last one showed, usually gets real improvement. Watching at 1.5x still catches pacing problems and saves time.

questions.prompt: Your stories feel solid. What's the next drill?
options: Write a brand-new story for every question
Re-record the same stories ten more times
Stop — the stories are ready
Random questions: decode, pick a story, deliver aloud
questions.explanation: The real interview tests the reflex: question → signal → story → CARL. When a type of question keeps landing on a weak story, that's a gap to fill before the real thing.

questions.prompt: You use an AI to mock-interview you. What is it genuinely good for?
options: Surfacing unexpected follow-ups on your stories
Replacing human mocks entirely
Simulating real pressure and nonverbal cues
Telling you if you'll get the offer
questions.explanation: Most candidates rehearse the opening and get caught by the follow-ups. AI can't give you live pressure, real interruptions, or a read of the room, which is why human mocks still matter.

questions.prompt: A friend agrees to mock-interview you. How do you set them up to actually help?
options: Ask them to be encouraging so you feel confident
Varied questions, a simple rubric, permission to be blunt
Give them only your strongest question type
Let them wing it with no guidance
questions.explanation: Spread the questions across signal areas, give them a 1-5 rubric (structure, story choice, depth, delivery), ask for real follow-ups, and ask for honest critique, not reassurance.

questions.prompt: It's interview morning. How do you spend the time?
options: Run three full mock interviews
Write a brand-new backup story
One quiet read-through of your stories and notes
Learn one more framework to be safe
questions.explanation: No new material. Confidence comes from repetition you've already done, and cramming just adds stress on top of it.

questions.prompt: You have only one evening before the interview. What does the course recommend?
options: Rewrite every story from scratch
Compress the ladder, don't skip practice entirely
Book a professional mock and nothing else
Skip practice — there isn't enough time
questions.explanation: One day of solo practice beats walking into a mock cold, and a 30-minute peer mock beats none at all.

questions.prompt: Which story deserves the most extra practice?
options: The Big Three — TMAY, flagship project, conflict
Your oldest story, since you remember it least
Your rarest, most unusual story
Whichever one is shortest
questions.explanation: They come up almost every time. Practice them until you can tell them conversationally without notes. TMAY's first 20 seconds set the tone for the whole interview.

questions.prompt: What does a professional mock give you that a peer can't?
options: Calibration against real hire/no-hire bars
Encouragement during a stressful process
Someone to ask you follow-up questions
Live pressure from a human listener
questions.explanation: A peer gives you pressure, follow-ups, and encouragement too. The professional's extra value is pattern-matching you against many real candidates at your target level.

questions.prompt: During a peer mock, you notice you say "basically" constantly. When did you probably first notice?
options: Reading the course notes
Thinking through the story silently
Watching a recording — most people never hear it live
Writing the story down on paper
questions.explanation: Filler words are invisible from the inside. That's why recording yourself, and recording mocks with permission, matters so much.

questions.prompt: Your conflict story, rehearsed, comes out sounding flat and bland. What's the fix?
options: Switch to a lower-stakes conflict
Speed up so it ends sooner
Remove even more of the emotional detail
Keep it professional, but leave the real emotion in
questions.explanation: A conflict story needs believable emotion, delivered in an even tone. Sanding it down for safety takes out the evidence that you can handle hard moments.
